Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 5:46: And when a loss occurs to a person's money in a matter not between him and his fellow, such as his ship being wrecked and the like, he should accept the judgment of Heaven with love, and think of what Job said (Job 1:21), "naked I came from my mother's womb." And we have seen fit to explain some words of this verse, according to our limited understanding, because of the benefit for practice that follows from it. The matter of "naked I came" is to teach that a person has no bond or connection to his own money at all - for just as he came into this world naked of all wealth, so he shall return to his grave naked of the world's wealth. And the word "shamah" [there, in the fuller verse "naked I shall return there"], according to the plain sense, is imprecise, but according to the secret it is precise, good, and fitting, and there is no room here to elaborate on its secret. Behold, one argument, that it is not fitting to worry over the loss of money, since ultimately he must leave it against his will, and it neither adds nor detracts for his soul's benefit. If you say, money is good for whoever merits it, since he has the ability to do good to the poor and to Torah scholars and to widows and orphans - therefore it says, "the LORD gave and the LORD has taken away," for when He gave it to him, He gave it in the attribute of mercy, and when He took it, He and His court took it - and had it appeared to Him and His court that the money would have been good for him and his soul, He would not have taken it from him. And further, it intended, in saying "the LORD gave," why should a person complain over what is not his own? And this is "the LORD gave" - and it is from His hand that everything comes, as King David, peace be upon him, said (I Chronicles 29:14), "for everything is from You, and from Your own hand we have given You." "And the LORD has taken away" - to teach that a person should not complain about the deed of the supernal court, which is He, blessed be He, for "righteousness and justice are the foundation of His throne" - shall the clay say to its potter, what are You doing? "Blessed be the name of the LORD" - for a person is obligated to bless over the bad just as he blesses over the good (Berachot, chapter 9, mishnah 5), and the reason is that His judgments with us are for our own good, to purify our souls, as it says (Psalms 145:9), "the LORD is good to all, and His mercies are over all His works." And for this reason Nachum Ish Gam Zu would say, "this too is for the good" (Ta'anit 21a) - and my teacher, peace be upon him, explained "gam zu" [this too]: although it is judgment, [he says it is] for the good, which is Chesed, to bind judgment forever with love, which is Chesed - and this is likewise "blessed be the name of the LORD," for blessing is on the right (Zohar, Parashat Ki Tisa, page 192a).
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 5:47: Further, among the corruptions that follow from anger, it is written in a book of ethics found among us in manuscript (Orchot Tzaddikim, gate 12): the first, that if he is a teacher of students, out of his anger the students fear to ask him their questions, lest he become angry with them - and even if they do ask, he does not explain to his students all that is needed, and answers them in an angry manner, and through this they do not understand - and this is what it said (Avot, chapter 2, mishnah 5), "nor is an exacting person a [good] teacher."
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 5:48: The angry person has no favor in the eyes of people, and is like a fool in their eyes, and through this his deeds are not accepted in people's eyes, and even if he has Torah and good deeds, no one learns from him. Rav Safra expounded, an irritable person achieves nothing but his own irritability (see Kiddushin, end, 40b). The angry person does not overlook wrongs and does not forgive his own insult, but always holds a grudge and takes vengeance. Anger brings a person to strife, for when he is angry at his fellows, they quarrel with him and he with them, and when there is strife, his enemies become envious of him - you already know the evil of strife, as it shall be explained at the time of strife.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 5:49: The angry person withholds his heart from all good, for when he is angry he has no heart to have mercy on the poor - for of the Name it is said (Habakkuk 3:2), "in wrath, remember mercy" - and this is far from people's ways. Anger nullifies a person's heart in prayer, and they said, the Shechinah does not rest in the midst of anger, for no angry person shall ever be a great sage, since anger drives wisdom from his heart, so that he does not answer properly and does not rebuke properly, and all his words are without intelligence.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 5:50: The angry person is withheld from discipline and rebukes, for no one is permitted to reveal his errors and disgraceful ways to him, since everyone refrains from telling him his own faults, lest he become enraged at him - and even if people do rebuke him, he does not accept their words because of his anger. In sum, an angry person accepts no good attribute unless he removes anger from his heart.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 5:51: Just as the angry person does not accept rebuke from others, so he cannot rebuke others - for the Torah said (Leviticus 19:17), "you shall surely rebuke your fellow, and not bear sin because of him." The beginning of rebuke should be calm and private, and you shall speak to him in a gentle tongue and with pleading, since you speak to him for his own good, and then you shall not bear sin because of him - but if you rebuke your fellow with a loud, angry voice, then you shall bear sin because of him, for he becomes ashamed, and that fellow shall not accept the rebuke - for such is the way of people: when a person comes upon his fellow forcefully, his fellow hardens himself against him and shall not humble himself before him. And of this Solomon said (Ecclesiastes 9:17), "the words of the wise, spoken calmly, are heard." And you already know of Hillel and Shammai: Shammai was exacting, and Hillel was humble - the converts said, the exactingness of Shammai sought to drive us from the world, but the humility of Hillel drew us near beneath the wings of the Shechinah (Shabbat 31a). Hillel, from the abundance of his humility, no one could make him angry, for whoever restrains himself from anger acquires the attribute of humility and compassion - for from the wrath of the LORD's anger comes immediate cruelty, as it is written (Exodus 22:23), "and My anger shall burn, and I will kill you with the sword" - and therefore vengeance is always written next to wrath, as it is written (Deuteronomy 11:17), "and the LORD's anger shall burn against you, and He shall shut up the heavens," and so on, and many similar cases.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 5:52: Anger causes brazenness in a person, for out of anger he does not submit and does not admit the truth. And the sage said, when you wish to associate with a person, provoke him to anger - if he admits the truth to you at the time of his anger, associate with him; if not, leave him alone.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 5:53: Anger brings a person to error - for who was greater than Moses, who became angry in three places and came to a general error, as it is said, "and Moses was angry with them," and it is written (Leviticus 10:16), "and he was angry with Elazar and with Itamar," and it is written (ibid. 10:17), "why have you not eaten the sin-offering," and it is written (Numbers 20:10), "listen now, you rebels," and so on, and it is written (ibid. 20:11), "and he struck the rock," and it is written (Numbers 31:14), "and Moses was angry with the officers of the army," and it is written after it (ibid. 31:21), "and Elazar the priest said, this is the statute of the law" - teaching that the halachah had been forgotten by Moses. And now you can understand: if this happened to Moses, who was the father of the wise, what shall happen to fools every day? Therefore Solomon said (Ecclesiastes 7:9), "do not hasten in your spirit to become angry."
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 5:54: And be very careful that no corruption occur during anger, for our Rabbis, of blessed memory, said (Shabbat 105b), one who tears his garments, or breaks his vessels, or scatters his money in his rage, shall be in your eyes as though he worships idolatry - for such is the craft of the evil inclination: today it tells him, do such-and-such, and tomorrow it tells him, do such-and-such and worship idolatry, and he worships - as it is written (Psalms 81:10), "there shall be no foreign god within you" - and what is the "foreign god" that is within a person's own body? Say, this is the evil inclination that incites a person at the time of his anger.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 5:55: And our Rabbis, of blessed memory, said (Avot, chapter 5, mishnah 11): four dispositions of temperament: easily angered and easily appeased - his loss is offset by his gain; hard to appease and hard to anger - his gain is offset by his loss; easily angered and hard to appease - wicked; hard to anger and easily appeased - pious. And these four dispositions are said of the righteous when they are angry at the good, or in worldly matters - but "easily angered at those who commit transgressions and easily appeased toward them" is a bad disposition, since he is appeased toward the wicked - and all the more so whoever is easily angered at the righteous and hard to anger at the wicked, easily appeased toward the wicked and hard to appease toward the righteous - this is a wholly wicked person.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 5:56: And although anger is a very bad attribute, nevertheless a person must at times conduct himself with the attribute of anger, such as to discipline the wicked, cast fear upon the people of his household, and instill fear in his students. And when he is angry at those who commit transgressions, he should weigh his anger, as it were, on a scale - since Moses our teacher, peace be upon him, said of Reuben and Gad (Numbers 32:14), "a brood of sinful men" - therefore his grandson became a priest for idols; and even though he becomes angry for the sake of Heaven, everything requires a good measure, in all a person's ways, and he should see how to perform a mitzvah both in his anger and in his laughter. A person who has the attribute of anger and forces his own disposition and conduct as though he were not angry and were not among the angry, of him it is said (Proverbs 16:32), "better slow to anger than a mighty man" - and "slow to anger" is one of the Thirteen Attributes said of the Holy One, blessed be He.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 5:57: And the sage said, one whose anger comes upon him with forethought shows settled judgment; one whose anger comes upon him without forethought shows folly. And further they said, whoever is a strongly angry and irritable person is not far from the raving mad; and whoever is habitually angry has no true life and never rejoices - and since he does not rejoice, he does not accept any of his own occurrences with joy, and does not justify the judgment upon himself, and cannot serve the Name, blessed be He, with joy. When a person is fasting, or is in some other distress, then anger is readily found in his heart - therefore at such times he must be extra careful not to become angry. Silence nullifies anger, and so does a lowered voice - therefore, when a person sees his anger intensifying, he should be silent or speak calmly, and not raise his voice in his anger, for raising one's voice at the time of anger arouses the anger further, but a lowered voice and silence quiet the anger - and also he should not look at the face of the person he is angry with, but speak with him without seeing his face, and then he shall drive his anger from his heart.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 5:58: And know that a person's completion is when he rules over his own anger, as it is said (Proverbs 19:11), "a man's intelligence makes him slow to anger." And anger tends greatly toward pride, and you already know the evils of pride. And it is fitting for a person to distance himself from anger even over a matter he might rightly be angry about - nevertheless he should restrain his spirit and not become angry. And an angry person must, first, when it occurs to his mind not to become angry, feel nothing at all - even if he is rebuked and cursed, he should not respond and should not become angry and should not be concerned - and this is clear: whoever was very exacting, it is easier for him to not feel it at all and be silent and restrain his spirit entirely, than for one who becomes only a little angry to do this - for the exacting person cannot do this at all, since if he draws a little anger into his heart, in the end it becomes much.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 5:59: And whoever wishes to restrain his spirit from anger, and yet wishes to cast fear upon the people of his household, or if he is a communal leader and wishes to be angry at the community so as to bring them back to the good - how shall he do it? He should show himself before them as though he were angry, in order to discipline them, while his own mind remains settled within himself, like a person who shows that he is angry at the time of his anger while he is not actually angry. And when he shows his anger toward the people of his household, he should be careful not to do so when he has poor guests, for they might think he is angry at them - therefore he should show himself joyful before them.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 5:60: And the Sages commanded to distance oneself from anger to the point that a person conducts himself so as not to feel even provoking matters, until anger is uprooted from his heart - and this is the good way and the way of the righteous, for they are insulted and do not insult, hear their own disgrace and do not respond, and rejoice in sufferings and justify the judgment upon themselves - and of them Scripture says (Judges 5:31), "and those who love Him are like the sun going forth in its might."
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 6:1: Although in the previous chapter we explained the causes that nullify anger, and it appeared, at first glance, that for the acquisition of humility it suffices to nullify anger, since from the negative you infer the positive - nevertheless one must know that for the acquisition of humility, many things are needed, for there are levels - and the proof of this is that Scripture said (Proverbs 22:4), "the reward of humility is the fear of the LORD" - meaning, the end of the levels of humility is the fear of the LORD, just as the heel [ekev] is the end of a person's body - and since this is so, it has many levels that require explanation.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 6:2: The first stage of acquiring humility is that he accustom himself to acquire the four attributes mentioned in the Mishnah, in Tractate Avot, at the beginning of the chapter of Ben Zoma (chapter 4): who is wise? He who learns from every person. Who is mighty? He who subdues his inclination. Who is rich? He who is happy with his portion. Who is honored? He who honors [other] creatures, and so on. And these four attributes correspond to the four letters of the Name, and with a little examination the reader familiar with the words of Rashbi, peace be upon him, shall know how each designation is correct in its place. And concerning the matter of humility, without doubt whoever learns from every person is certainly humble, for out of the abundance of his humility he does not hesitate to learn Torah even from the smallest of the small, since he cares only for the honor of Torah - and this is (Psalms 119:99), "for Your testimonies are my meditation" - and so it says in the Zohar (Parashat Acharei Mot, page 69a), that we have learned, whoever pays heed to the words of Torah is happy in this world, as though he received the Torah from Sinai, and even from every person one should also hear words of Torah, and whoever bends his ear to it gives honor to the Holy King and gives honor to Torah - and of him it is written (Deuteronomy 27:9), "this day you have become a people to the LORD your God."
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 6:3: Who is mighty? He who subdues his inclination - as explained, "better slow to anger than a mighty man" - for if they disgrace and provoke him, he is slow to anger, subdues his inclination, and is silent - this is the true mighty one, and he is better than the mighty one called mighty in matters of war. And concerning the proof, one can say that the proof from the verse is that since the verse said "better slow to anger than a mighty man," it does not say "better this than that" unless they fall into the same category - it appears from this that the slow-to-anger person is also mighty, and he is fittingly called mighty since he performs a greater feat of might in subduing his own inclination than the mighty one who wages the wars of nations. And this is one of the attributes of humility, namely being slow to anger. And he is called "mighty," subduing his inclination, because the inclination is drawn below from the dross of gold, and he subdues it and does not let it spread - along the lines of what is explained in the Tikkunim (page 12a), that it is like a dog kept subdued in chains.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 6:4: Who is rich? He who is happy with his portion - for it is one of the attributes of humility to content oneself with little, as explained in the first chapter of this Gate, that this is one of the attributes of Abraham our father, peace be upon him: a good eye, a lowly spirit, and so on (Avot, chapter 5, mishnah 19) - and whoever pursues excess, his heart becomes proud, as it is written (Deuteronomy 8:12-14), "lest you eat and be satisfied and build fine houses and dwell in them... and your heart become proud, and you forget the LORD your God."
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 6:5: Who is honored? He who honors [other] creatures - this too is one of the attributes of humility, to honor all creatures, poor and rich alike, since all are made in the supernal image, and whoever honors them honors the Craftsman who made them, and whoever disgraces them, God forbid, disgraces the Craftsman - and as they said in Ta'anit (20b) concerning Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar, who said, how ugly is this man - he said to him, go tell the craftsman who made me, how ugly is this vessel You have made - until he had to ask his forgiveness, and he said to him, I forgive you, forgive me, and so on - and this is the teaching of Bereishit Rabbah we copied in the previous chapter on the verse "this is the book of the generations of Adam"; see there. And in honoring every person, small and great alike, this excludes the proud, for the proud person shows in himself that honor is fitting for him and that the rest of people are inferior to him in his eyes, and he does not honor them - and his proof is the verse (I Samuel 2:30), "for those who honor Me I shall honor" - and Rabbeinu Ovadiah, peace be upon him, explained: "for those who honor Me I shall honor" - and this is an a fortiori argument: if the Holy One, blessed be He, who is the King of Glory, and everything He created in His world He created only for His glory, [still] honors those who honor Him, all the more so [should] flesh and blood - to this point.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 6:6: And close to the explanation I have explained, I found that the pious Rabbi Yosef Yavetz, peace be upon him, explained - these are its words: and know that these four merits are the whole perfection of man. The first is the merit of wisdom; the second and third are the merits of action - the second, negative commandments, and the third, [positive] action - and as they said (Berachot 8a), greater is one who enjoys the fruit of his own labor than one who fears Heaven, as I have already introduced. And the fourth is the most excellent of all, when all of them are in their perfection - for when all of them gather and unite in a complete unity, then humility is unified from them, which is greater than all the other merits, and as they said (Avodah Zarah 20b), humility is greater than all of them, and it is what brings to the Holy Spirit, and it is written (Proverbs 16:32/18:12), "and before honor comes humility." And for this Ben Zoma called him "honored" - for the glory of the LORD hovers over him all day, and dwells between his shoulders, and these draw one another along. For wisdom - one who knows the merit of his own soul and its measure shall not sell it for momentary pleasure - a parable of two people who each had a fine pearl: the one who knows the pearl's worth guards it like the apple of his eye; the one who does not know its worth gives it away for a loaf of bread. And so the boorish do not feel the merit of their own soul, and therefore send themselves into transgressions - but the intelligent person, careful for his soul, guards it, and the fear of Heaven enters his heart - wisdom, by its power, weakens the power of the evil inclination, and from the side of fear the power of love begins to sparkle within him, for fear and love, both as one, bound together, shall unite and not separate. And also, from his subduing his own inclination, he contents himself with little, and it shall be good in his eyes to give his tithe to whoever is entrusted to him. And behold, one who does good to people with his money, all the more so with the sweetness of his tongue - it follows that these four merits draw one another along - to this point.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 6:7: Now, along the lines of "who is honored" that the pious author mentioned, peace be upon him, explained, that it is the secret of supernal glory - and so it is also, by my own approach, understood, what they said in Eruvin (13b) - these are their words - concerning what it said there, why did they merit to establish the halachah like Beit Hillel? Because they were pleasant and were insulted [without insulting] - to teach you that whoever lowers himself, the Holy One, blessed be He, raises him up, and whoever raises himself, the Holy One, blessed be He, lowers him; whoever pursues greatness, greatness flees from him, and whoever flees from greatness, greatness pursues him; and whoever pushes the moment, the moment pushes him back, and whoever is pushed aside because of the moment, the moment stands ready for him - to this point. And Rashi, peace be upon him, explained: "pushes the moment" - toils to become wealthy and great and sees that he does not succeed, but nevertheless goes about seeking far and wide and brings himself into loftiness. "The moment stands ready" - after a time, a successful moment is destined to stand ready for him.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 6:8: The reason for the matter, that whoever lowers himself, the Holy One, blessed be He, raises him up, and the rest of this teaching's words, is as we explained in the first chapter of this Gate: that the Shechinah rests only upon a broken and crushed heart, and the poor, who are "her broken vessels" (Zohar, Parashat Vayikra, page 9a), are her throne, as it says (Isaiah 57:15), "high and holy I dwell, and with the contrite and humble of spirit." And we explained in the Gate of Repentance (chapter 4) that as the moon is filled and renewed, those who hold fast to her are renewed and ascend with her - and whoever does the opposite, his spirit becomes proud over him, and the Shechinah distances itself from him, and then greatness too flees from him - for when the Holy One, blessed be He, is pleased with a person and rests upon him, He gives him favor in the eyes of people, that they honor him and exalt him; but when the Holy One, blessed be He, is not with him, people too distance themselves from him - along the lines of "whoever is pleasing to the Omnipresent's spirit is pleasing to people's spirit," and so on (Avot, chapter 3, mishnah 10) - therefore, "when the LORD is pleased with a man's ways, He makes even his enemies be at peace with him" (Proverbs 16:7). And along these lines, [greatness] is called "greatness" from the aspect of Gedulah [Chesed], and it is called "the moment" [sha'ah], as explained in the Tikkunim, these designations for it - and therefore the secret of supernal greatness flees from him, and likewise "the moment pushes him" or "a moment stands ready for him."
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 6:9: And through this, several verses in Proverbs concerning humility are understood. The first (Proverbs 15:33), "and before honor comes humility" - meaning, before supernal honor rests upon a person, he must be humble, for the reason stated. And likewise (ibid. 29:23), "and he who is lowly of spirit shall obtain honor" - for through lowliness of spirit he becomes a throne for the Shechinah, and he supports her, along the lines of a chair that supports a person. And likewise (ibid. 20:3), "it is honor for a man to cease from strife" - meaning, the drawing of supernal honor to a man is when he ceases from strife, but if he is a man of strife and a master of dispute, supernal honor flees from him. And therefore, in order to merit the attribute of supernal honor, one must take hold of all the attributes of humility found explained in the verses and in the Gemara.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 6:10: And besides what was explained in the previous chapters, we find several further conditions, and these are they. The first: submission in all his worldly affairs, the revealed and the hidden among them, in his speech, in his deeds, and in the movement of his organs and their powers - and his inner self should not, in all this, be the opposite of his outer appearance, nor his private thoughts contrary to what appears of him - and his movements should be measured, correct, and even, going along the path of submission and lowliness toward God, blessed be He, and toward people according to the differences in their levels, and according to what is good for him from them for his Torah and his world, as it is said (Psalms 112:5), "good is the man who deals graciously and lends, who conducts his affairs with justice" - and the Sages said (Avot, chapter 4, mishnah 10), "and be lowly of spirit before every person," and they said (chapter 3, mishnah 12), "be pliable [lit. light] to a leader and easy to the youth" - to this point, from Chovot HaLevavot (Gate of Submission, chapter 6).
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 6:11: And of this category is what they said in Sanhedrin (88b): they sent from there, who is a person of the World to Come? Whoever is humble and lowly, bows to enter and bows to leave, studies Torah constantly, and does not take credit for himself - the Rabbis fixed their eyes upon Rav Ulla bar Abba - to this point. And Rashi, peace be upon him, explained "bows" - he stoops when entering and stoops when leaving, and so on.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 6:12: Further, at the end he used to recite (Berachot 17a) - a saying often in Abaye's mouth: a person should always be shrewd in fear [of Heaven], and a gentle answer turns away wrath, and increase peace with his brothers and relatives and with every person, even with a Gentile in the marketplace, so that he be beloved above and cherished below, and accepted by people. They said of Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai that no person ever greeted him first, even a Gentile in the marketplace - to this point.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 6:13: And so we learn in Avot, chapter 4 (mishnah 15): Rabbi Matya ben Charash says, be first to greet every person, and be a tail to lions rather than a head to foxes. And he explained the reason for "be a tail to lions rather than a head to foxes": because the tail of a lion is called a lion, and the head of a fox is a fox.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 6:14: And likewise, among the conditions of lowliness is that one be among the disciples of Aaron, loving peace and pursuing peace (Avot, chapter 1, mishnah 12) - and they explained in the Baraita of Tractate Kallah (chapter 3) that lowliness of spirit is learned from Aaron, as it is written (Malachi 2:7), "for the priest's lips shall guard knowledge" - and there is no one more lowly of spirit than a pursuer of peace, and consider in your own mind how one can pursue peace unless he is lowly of spirit - how so? If a person curses him, he says to him, peace be upon you; if a person quarrels with him, he is silent. And further, if two are quarreling, he lowers his own spirit and goes to this one and pleases him about that one, and likewise to that one - such was Aaron's craft. And the manner in which Aaron pursued peace is explained there, and copied in Menorat HaMaor of Rabbi Yitzchak Aboab, peace be upon him (Ner 6, Klal 2, chapter 2), and therefore we shall not be lengthy in copying its words.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 6:15: And further, under this category of submission: that when he sits among people, he should choose for himself the lowliest of the places - and so they said in Vayikra Rabbah (1:5): Rabbi Yehoshua of Sichnin in the name of Rabbi Levi opened the verse (Proverbs 25:7), "for it is better that he say to you, come up here, than to be put lower before a noble." Rabbi Akiva taught it in the name of Rabbi Shimon ben Azzai: distance yourself from your place two or three seats and sit until they say to you, come up here - and do not go up so that they say to you, go down - it is better that they say to you, go up, go up, than that they say to you, go down, go down. And so Hillel says, my own lowering is my raising, and my raising is my lowering - what is the reason? "He who raises Himself to dwell on high, [yet] He lowers Himself [to look]" (Psalms 113:5-6). You find that at the time the Holy One, blessed be He, revealed Himself to Moses from within the thornbush, he was hiding his face from Him, as it is said (Exodus 3:6), "and Moses hid his face" - the Holy One, blessed be He, said to him (ibid. 3:10), "come, and I will send you to Pharaoh" - to this point.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 6:16: Further, they said in the Midrash Mechilta (BaChodesh, chapter 3): Rabbi Yosei says, it is not the place that honors a person, but a person who honors his place - from here they said, all the time the Shechinah rests on the mountain, "whoever touches the mountain shall surely be put to death" (Exodus 19:12) - once the Shechinah departs, all are permitted to go up the mountain - to this point.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 6:17: And likewise, under this category is that a person minimize his own affairs, as they expounded in Bereishit Rabbah (chapter 6:4): why was he called Yoktan? Because he minimized himself and his affairs. And what did he merit? He merited to establish thirteen families. And if the small one, who minimizes his affairs, [merits this], all the more so a great one who minimizes his affairs. And similarly (Genesis 48:14), "and Israel stretched out his right hand and placed it on Ephraim's head, though he was the younger" - Rabbi Chananya said, do we not already know from the genealogy that he was the younger? Rather, it means that he minimized his affairs - and what did he merit? He merited the birthright. And if the younger one, through minimizing his affairs, merited the birthright, all the more so a great one who minimizes his affairs.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 6:18: Further, concerning the merit of one who minimizes himself, it is explained in the Zohar (Parashat Shelach Lecha, page 168a), and these are innovations that the souls of the righteous told Rashbi, peace be upon him, from the academy on high - these are its words: if, Rabbi, how many new teachings from the great academy! Happy is he who makes himself small in this world - how great and supernal he is in that world - and thus the head of the academy opened: whoever is small is great, and whoever is great is small, as it is written (Genesis 23:1), "and the life of Sarah was a hundred years and twenty years and seven years" - "a hundred," which is a great number, has "year" written of it [diminished, singular]; the smallness of the years, He diminished it. "Seven," which is a small number, He enlarged and made great, for it is written "years" [plural]. Come and see, the Holy One, blessed be He, makes great only whoever makes himself small, and makes small only whoever He makes great - happy is he who makes himself small in this world, how great is his exaltation in that world - to this point.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 6:19: And so our Rabbis, of blessed memory, also expounded in Megillat Esther, on the verse (Ezekiel 21:31), "remove the turban" - Rabbi Yochanan and Rabbi Shimon ben Lakish: "remove the turban" - whoever is great in this world is small in the World to Come. Rabbi Miyasha bar Miyasha, grandson of Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi, fell silent during his illness for three days; after three days his mind settled upon him. His father said to him, where were you, my son? He said to him, I was in a topsy-turvy world. What did you see there? He said, I saw many people, here in honor and there in disgrace, there in honor and here in disgrace - to this point.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 6:20: And further, among the conditions of humility is to receive every person with joy, with a pleasant countenance, and to be first to greet every person - and if he speaks with his fellow, he should not speak with an angry face but with a smiling face - and our Rabbis, of blessed memory, explained in Ketubot (111b), on the verse (Genesis 49:12), "and teeth white [levan] from milk" - these are their words: Rabbi says, better is one who whitens [malbin] his teeth to his fellow [i.e., shows him a friendly smile] than one who gives him milk to drink, as it is said, "and teeth white from milk" - do not read "white [levan]" but "whitening [libun] of teeth" - to this point.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 6:21: And likewise he should not refrain from speaking and responding to whoever comes first, even if he is the smallest of the small - and this is learned from the story of Hillel the Elder, brought in Shabbat, chapter 2 (31a), that Hillel said to him, sit, and he would respond to him on every single matter, and did not say, I have no time now, come tomorrow, or other excuses. And similarly to this we find with Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi, whom a child called and he walked after him three miles' distance, as found in the Midrash and copied in the Yalkut on Isaiah (siman 478), on the verse (Isaiah 54:12), "and I will make your battlements of rubies [kadkod]."
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 6:22: Further, among the conditions of humility, the author of Chovot HaLevavot wrote (Gate of Submission, chapter 6), that it is to do good for people, speak well of them, judge them favorably, not speak of their disgrace, and forgive them what they speak and tell of his own disgrace, even if they are not deserving of this. And concerning forgiving evil speech and disgrace, what Scripture said (Numbers 12:1), "and Miriam and Aaron spoke against Moses," and it says (ibid. 12:3), "and the man Moses was very humble" - because he forgave them. And it said (Psalms 7:5), "if I have repaid evil to him who was at peace with me," and it says (Proverbs 24:29), "do not say, as he did to me, so I shall do to him" - and they, of blessed memory, said (Gittin 36b), the insulted who do not insult, who hear their own disgrace and do not respond, who act out of love and rejoice in sufferings - of them Scripture says (Judges 5:31), "and those who love Him are like the sun going forth in its might" - to this point.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 6:23: And what follows from this is that he should not bring a lawsuit against his fellow [before Heaven, i.e. complain to God], as we learn at the end of the chapter "HaChovel" (Bava Kama 93a): Rabbi Yochanan said, whoever brings a judgment against his fellow [before Heaven] is punished first, as it is said (Genesis 16:5), "and Sarai said to Abram, my wrong be upon you," and it is written (ibid. 23:2), "and Abraham came to eulogize Sarah and to weep for her" - and this applies when he has a judge on earth [and could have sought justice there instead]. Rabbi Yitzchak said, woe to the one who cries out more than to the one cried out against. It is likewise taught: both the one who cries out and the one cried out against are meant, but they hasten [punishment] for the one who cries out more than for the one cried out against - to this point. And Rashi explained: "both the one who cries out and the one cried out against are meant" - "and My anger shall burn, and I will kill you" (Exodus 22:23) implies two, but they hasten from the one who cries out first, as we find with Sarah - to this point. And I heard the reason for this from my teacher, peace be upon him: it is not fitting to arouse judgment above, for the King should always be in good favor with everyone, and whoever brings a lawsuit arouses accusation and judgment above, and the King becomes angry to execute judgment - and it is written (Proverbs 16:14), "the king's wrath is like messengers of death" - and therefore they exact punishment from the one who cries out first, because he aroused the judgment that had been quiet - and this is along the lines of (Ecclesiastes 10:8), "he who digs a pit shall fall into it." And for this reason Mar Zutra used to say, every night before he slept, I forgive whoever has caused me distress - as we say in Megillah, chapter "Bnei Ha'ir" (28a), "and my fellow's curse never went up on my bed" - for so did Mar Zutra, when he went up to his bed, say, I forgive whoever has caused me distress - to this point - so that he not be the cause of arousing judgment to strike any creature. And this is the attribute of the pious, which is beyond the letter of the law - for although he had not cried out over a matter for which he had no [earthly] recourse, and for which he was permitted to cry out, nevertheless he would forgive.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 6:24: And so it is fitting to be careful not to provoke one's fellow, so as not to come to mishap - for sometimes the curse of an ordinary person is fulfilled, as we learn there (Bava Kama 93a) - these are their words: and Rabbi Yitzchak said, a person should never take the curse of an ordinary person lightly - for Abimelech cursed Sarah, and it was fulfilled in her offspring, as it is said (Genesis 20:16), "behold, it is for you a covering of the eyes" - he said to her, since you covered from me and did not reveal that he was your husband, and caused me this distress, may it be [God's] will that you have children with covered eyes - and it was fulfilled in her offspring, as it is written (ibid. 27:1), "and it came to pass, when Isaac was old, that his eyes were too dim to see" - to this point. And further there, Rabbi Abahu said, a person should always be among the pursued rather than the pursuers, for there is no bird more pursued than doves and pigeons, yet Scripture made them fit for the altar - to this point.
